specAnchors.text: understand the following reactions: i solid Group 1 halides with concentrated sulfuric acid, to illustrate the trend in reducing ability of the hydrogen halides ii precipitation reactions of the aqueous anions Cl - , Br - and I - with aqueous silver nitrate solution and nitric acid, and the solubility of the precipitates in aqueous ammonia solution iii hydrogen halides with ammonia gas (to produce ammonium halides) and with water (to produce acids)

be able to make predictions about fluorine and astatine and their compounds, in terms of knowledge of trends in halogen chemistry Further suggested practicals: i reaction of solid potassium halides with concentrated sulfuric acid ii precipitation reaction for halides and other anions

primer.text: Concentrated sulfuric acid tests halide grit: chloride only steams, bromide turns the acid to choking dioxide, and iodide pushes sulfur all the way to stinking hydrogen sulfide. This note also equips you with the silver nitrate test and the fluorine and astatine prediction patterns.

modules.title: Halide ions versus concentrated sulfuric acid: the chloride story
sourceHeadings: Reaction of chloride ions with concentrated sulfuric acid
modules.opening: Add concentrated sulfuric acid to a solid halide and a toxic gas leaves the test tube. For chloride the story stops at hydrogen chloride - misty fumes in moist air - because chloride is the weakest reducing agent of the trio.
keyPoints: Halide ions meeting concentrated sulfuric acid give off toxic gases, so the reactions belong in a fume cupboard.
The general step is H2SO4 + X- -> HX + HSO4-, producing the hydrogen halide.
With sodium chloride the product is hydrogen chloride gas, seen as misty fumes: H2SO4 + NaCl -> HCl + NaHSO4.
Concentrated sulfuric acid is not reduced by chloride, so the chloride reaction stops at the hydrogen halide.

low.restatement: Every halide first grabs a proton from sulfuric acid to make the hydrogen halide; with chloride nothing further happens - just misty HCl fumes in the moist air.
low.analogy: A weak thief (chloride) picks the pocket (proton) but cannot rob the vault (the acid's own atoms) - the strongest acid reagent stays intact.
low.examPointer: State the observation 'misty fumes of hydrogen chloride' and write the NaCl equation with NaHSO4 as the second product.

medium.restatement: The first step is acid-base: the halide acts as a base, taking H+ from H2SO4 to give HX and HSO4-. Chloride's low reducing power means no subsequent redox with the acid, which is why only steamy fumes appear.
medium.analogy: The first handshake (proton transfer) completes; the stronger handshake (electron transfer) never happens for chloride.
medium.examPointer: Do not invent bromine or sulfur dioxide for the chloride tube - those belong to bromide and iodide.

modules.title: Bromide and iodide: the acid gets reduced
sourceHeadings: Reaction of bromide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid
Reaction of iodide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid
modules.opening: Down the group the halide's reducing power climbs. Bromide strips the acid down to sulfur dioxide and reddish-brown bromine; iodide goes further still, to sulfur, even to rotten-egg hydrogen sulfide, as violet iodine vapour pours out.
keyPoints: Hydrogen halides lose thermal stability descending the group, so HBr and HI decompose further.
Bromide: H2SO4 + NaBr -> HBr + NaHSO4, then 2HBr + H2SO4 -> Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O, giving a reddish-brown gas.
Iodide: HI is oxidised by the acid to I2 with SO2, then further to yellow solid sulfur (6HI) and to hydrogen sulfide (8HI).
Hydrogen sulfide betrays itself with a strong smell of bad eggs.

low.restatement: Bromide stops the acid at SO2 plus bromine vapour; iodide keeps going - SO2, then yellow sulfur, then stinking H2S - because iodide donates electrons ever more readily.
low.analogy: Bromide picks one lock; iodide is a master key opening the acid's vault down to the deepest (-2 sulfur) floor.
low.examPointer: Know all three iodide equations (2, 6, 8 HI) and the observations: purple vapour, yellow solid, bad-egg smell.

medium.restatement: Each hydrogen halide first forms as before; then the acid oxidises it while being reduced itself: sulfur +6 -> +4 (SO2), -> 0 (S), -> -2 (H2S). The iodide route reaches the deepest reduction because iodide is the strongest reducing agent here.
medium.analogy: The acid's sulfur atom descends a three-floor ladder (+6 to +4 to 0 to -2) as the halide climbs its own reactivity ladder.
medium.examPointer: Match each observation to its equation: SO2 choking gas, Br2 reddish-brown, I2 violet, S yellow solid, H2S bad eggs.

modules.title: The reducing-power ladder and the silver nitrate test
sourceHeadings: Explaining the Trend in Reducing Ability of Halide Ions
modules.opening: Two ladders meet here: halide reducing power climbing Cl- < Br- < I-, and the silver nitrate test reading back from precipitate colour and ammonia solubility to the halide identity.
keyPoints: Halide reducing power increases down the group as the ions get larger and their outer electrons are lost more readily.
Silver nitrate gives ionic AgX precipitates: Ag+ + X- -> AgX, in colours white (chloride), cream (bromide), pale yellow (iodide).
Ammonia distinguishes the precipitates: chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia, bromide only in concentrated, iodide in neither.

low.restatement: Bigger halide ions lose electrons more easily, so reducing power runs Cl- < Br- < I-. In testing, silver halide colours deepen from white through cream to pale yellow, and ammonia strength needed to dissolve them runs the same way down.
low.analogy: Three locks of increasing stubbornness: the chloride lock opens with a light key (dilute ammonia), bromide needs the heavy key, iodide refuses both.
low.examPointer: Quote the full test sequence - nitric acid, silver nitrate, then dilute then concentrated ammonia - and match every colour and solubility outcome.

medium.restatement: Electron loss ease grows with ionic radius because the outer electrons feel less nuclear pull; that is why iodide can reduce SO2 while chloride cannot. The silver test works independently of redox: Ag+ precipitates AgX, and ammonia complexes the silver, dissolving the precipitate according to halide.
medium.analogy: The ammonia key unlocks silver from its halide partner; the deeper the lock (heavier halide), the stronger the key needed.
medium.examPointer: Nitric acid first removes interfering ions such as carbonate - do not omit it in the written method.

modules.title: Hydrogen halides, fluorine and astatine predictions
modules.opening: Hydrogen halides are the group's acids in waiting: they meet ammonia to give ammonium salts and water to give the hydrohalic acids. Fluorine and astatine extend the ladder - with exceptions like soluble silver fluoride that keep predictions honest.
keyPoints: Halogen with hydrogen gives the hydrogen halide, e.g. Cl2 + H2 -> 2HCl.
Hydrogen halides react with ammonia to form ammonium halides, e.g. NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl.
In water, hydrogen chloride ionises into hydrochloric acid: HCl -> H+ + Cl-.
Silver fluoride is soluble, so silver nitrate cannot test for fluoride; predictions for astatine follow the group pattern.

low.restatement: Hydrogen halides split two ways: with ammonia they crystallise as ammonium salts; in water they ionise into the acids. Fluorine and astatine slots into the group pattern, with the noted silver fluoride exception.
low.analogy: One molecule, two doors: the ammonia door yields a solid salt, the water door yields free ions that conduct and turn litmus red.
low.examPointer: For astatide questions, mirror iodide chemistry and adjust one step down the group; remember AgF's solubility when asked about fluoride tests.

medium.restatement: Acid formation in water is ionisation: HX releases H+ (as H3O+) and X-. For hydrogen astatide the same pattern applies, HAt + H2O -> H3O+ + At-. The fluoride exception arises because AgF does not precipitate, so the standard halide test fails for fluoride.
medium.analogy: Every hydrogen halide drops its proton into water the same way; astatine is just the next rung of the same ladder.
medium.examPointer: Write astatide equations by pattern-matching iodide, and quote AgF(aq) as the soluble exception when fluoride testing is asked.

glossary.definition: A binary compound of hydrogen with a halogen, HX, which fumes in moist air and ionises to a hydrohalic acid in water.
A species that donates electrons to another species, reducing it while being oxidised itself.
The HSO4- ion left when sulfuric acid donates one proton to a halide ion.
The resistance of a hydrogen halide to decomposition; it decreases down the group, so HI breaks apart most readily.

workedExample.prompt: Hydrogen astatide gas is bubbled into water and an acid forms. Write the equation for the ionisation.
steps: Model the ionisation on hydrogen iodide: HI (g) + H2O (l) -> H3O+ (aq) + I- (aq).
Substitute astatine one place below iodine in the group pattern.
Check the charge ledger: neutral reactants give one positive and one negative ion, and H, O and At atom counts balance.
